lec05kp24-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp24-u01-p2-title.text: The product rule: minimising the mean KL distance gives the geometric mean of the probabilities

lec05kp24-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp24-u01-p2-bridge.text: Even the best classifier errs where others are right. How are the probabilities of several classifiers merged into one set?

lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-1.name: fig:lec05-kp24-product|Product rule: the posterior probability is a classifier's confidence in each class after seeing x; the KL distance measures how far two distributions are. Find the combined distribution P minimising the mean KL distance to the L classifiers: expand the mean; let Q_i=∏P_ji^(1/L)/C; substitute to get KL(P‖Q)−ln C; KL≥0, minimal at P=Q. Example: three classifiers (0.8,0.2), (0.6,0.4), (0.7,0.3): ω1 has product 0.336, ω2 has 0.024, so choose ω1.

lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-3.name: term:Posterior probability
lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-3.text:
posterior $P_j(\omega_i|x)$: how sure classifier $j$ is, after seeing $x$,
that it belongs to class $i$; the classes sum to 1.

lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-5.name: term:KL distance
lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-5.text:
KL distance $D(P\|P_j)=\sum_iP_i\ln(P_i/P_{ji})$: how far two distributions
are; asymmetric, strictly not a distance.

lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-2.name: term:Product rule
lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-2.text: product rule: multiply, take the $L$-th root, pick the largest: $P(\omega_i|x)=\frac{1}{C}\prod_{j}P_j^{1/L}$

lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-3.name: fig:lec05-kp24-product#37
lec05kp24-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp24-product-3.text: The product rule: the geometric mean, which minimises the mean KL distance.

lec05kp24-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp24-u01-p3-title.text: The sum rule: swapping the arguments of the KL distance gives the arithmetic mean

lec05kp24-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp24-u01-p3-bridge.text: The product rule minimises the mean KL distance and gives the geometric mean of the probabilities. What do we get if the two arguments of the KL distance are swapped?

lec05kp24-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp24-sum-1.name: fig:lec05-kp24-sum|Sum rule: swap the two arguments of the KL distance (P_j first); after averaging only −ΣP̄_i ln P_i depends on P, minimal at P=P̄, so the best solution is the arithmetic mean P=(1/L)ΣP_j. The same three classifiers give an average of 0.70 for ω1 and 0.30 for ω2: choose ω1 again. Each rule has a rigorous information-theoretic origin, so theory has no preference; the product is fragile when an output is near zero and in practice the sum is often steadier (source).

lec05kp24-u01-p8-nf-lec05-kp24-bayes-1.name: fig:lec05-kp24-bayes|Bayesian view: assuming the x_j seen by the classifiers are independent, the Bayes rule gives max_k P(ω_k)^(1−L) ∏_j P(ω_k|x_j), again a product rule, very sensitive to errors in the posterior estimates; the sum is more error-tolerant and often beats the product in practice (source). steps.label: Combining classifiers
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp24 with view-from-text-v2: the pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic, with the terms defined inside the same figure. 8 main pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). The experiments on pages 1, 6 and 7 (two-moon data, 25 bagged trees, 10-dimensional data) were designed for this lecture and generated by code; they are not the source's experiments. The source contributes the KL derivation of the product and sum rules, majority voting and the independence assumption, the three ways to make diversity, the Bayesian view and the handwritten-digit conclusions. On page 1, 85.15% and 86.15% sit on a rounding boundary; rounding is done only in the last step (85.2%, 86.2%). Two cells of the lecture's section 5 table had rounding errors and were corrected to 0.753 and 0.926. English version.

steps.label: Complementary information
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP24, following the bagging of KP23. The question: what do we gain by combining different classifiers? The setup was designed for this lecture and generated by code: the two-moon data of KP23, 100 training points per class and 2000 new points; three classifiers: logistic regression gets 1703 right, the depth-4 tree 1652, 3-NN 1756, and the vote of the three 1723, which is 85.2, 82.6, 87.8 and 86.2 percent; 85.15 and 86.15 sit on a rounding boundary and are rounded only in the last step. On the right look at the best, 3-NN: it errs on 244 points, and on 146 of them, about 60 percent, at least one other classifier is right; this is complementary information. But the vote of the three gets only 86.2 percent, still below the 87.8 percent of 3-NN: complementary information is worth something only if it can be extracted, and combining does not guarantee improvement. The next page asks how a set of probabilities from several classifiers is merged into one.

steps.label: The product rule
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that even the best classifier errs where others are right. This page asks how the probabilities of several classifiers are merged into one set. First two terms: the posterior probability is a classifier's confidence in each class after seeing x, with the classes summing to 1; the KL distance measures how far two distributions are, it is asymmetric and strictly speaking not a distance. The idea is to find a combined distribution P with the smallest mean KL distance to the L classifiers. Four derivation steps: expand the mean; let Q be the product of the classifiers' probabilities to the power 1 over L divided by C, where C makes it sum to 1; substitute, and the mean distance is the KL distance between P and Q minus ln C; the KL distance is always at least 0 and is 0 only when P equals Q, so the minimum is at P equal to Q. The result is the product rule: multiply the classifiers' probabilities, take the L-th root and pick the largest class. Example: three classifiers (0.8, 0.2), (0.6, 0.4), (0.7, 0.3): the product for omega 1 is 0.336 and for omega 2 is 0.024, so choose omega 1. The next page asks what we get if the two arguments of the KL distance are swapped.

steps.label: The sum rule
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page derived the product rule: minimising the mean KL distance gives the geometric mean of the probabilities. This page asks what we get when the two arguments of the KL distance are swapped. Swap the two arguments of Dj, putting Pj first. After averaging, only one term depends on P: minus the sum of the arithmetic mean P bar times ln P, which is smallest at P equal to P bar, a standard property of probability distributions. So the best solution is the arithmetic mean: P equals 1 over L times the sum of the classifiers' probabilities, which is the sum rule. For the same three classifiers omega 1 averages 0.70 and omega 2 gets 0.30, so omega 1 is chosen again. Each rule has a rigorous information-theoretic origin, so theory has no preference; the product derivation is clean but fragile when an output is near zero, and in practice the sum is often steadier, which is the source's remark. The next page asks when the two rules differ, for example when one extreme classifier appears.

steps.label: The veto
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the sum rule gives the arithmetic mean and the product rule the geometric mean. This page asks whether the two rules differ when one extreme classifier appears. The example was designed for this lecture: five classifiers give the correct class omega 1 the values 0.7, 0.7, 0.7, 0.7 and 0.001, the rest going to omega 2. Product: omega 1 is 0.7 to the fourth times 0.001, which is 0.00024; omega 2 is 0.3 to the fourth times 0.999, which is 0.00809, so omega 2 is chosen, wrong. Sum: omega 1 is 4 times 0.7 plus 0.001, divided by 5, which is 0.5602, and omega 2 is 0.4398, so omega 1 is chosen, right. Vote: 4 votes to 1, omega 1, right. One near-zero factor drags the whole product to zero, which is a veto. The next page asks how much voting helps, since voting is the simplest rule.

steps.label: Majority vote
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the product is vetoed while the vote is unaffected. This page asks how much the accuracy can rise when several classifiers vote. A majority vote decides only if at least l c classifiers agree; for odd L, l c is half of L plus 1. Assume the decisions are independent and every classifier has the same accuracy p; the probability that the majority is right is the binomial probability of at least l c right: the sum from m equal to l c to L of L choose m times p to the m times 1 minus p to the L minus m. Example: p equal to 0.6 and L equal to 3, so l c is 2: 3 times 0.6 squared times 0.4 plus 0.6 cubed, which is 0.432 plus 0.216, which is 0.648. The four lines in the chart are p equal to 0.6, 0.55, 0.5 and 0.45; with p equal to 0.6, L equal to 3, 11 and 51 give 0.648, 0.753 and 0.926; for p above 0.5 a larger L is better, for p below 0.5 it is worse, and p equal to 0.5 stays at 0.5. This holds under independence. The next page asks whether that independence holds for real classifiers.

steps.label: The illusion of independence
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page's formula says a larger L is better for p above 0.5, but it assumes independence. This page asks whether the decisions of real classifiers are independent. The experiment was designed for this lecture and generated by code: the two-moon data of KP23, 20 training sets with seeds 100 to 119, 25 bagged trees each with the entropy criterion and no depth limit; the new data are the same 2000 points as on the first page. The mean accuracy p of a single tree is 83.8%; plugging it into the independence formula P c of 25 and p predicts 99.99%; the actual majority vote gets only 87.7%; the fraction V of members that differ from the majority is 0.095. The gap is large because these trees are trained on resamples of the same data and their errors are highly shared. A common myth is that if every classifier beats guessing, the vote tends to 100%; it relies on independence, which does not hold in practice, and the larger L is the less realistic it is, as the source says. The next page asks how to make the members differ when independence cannot be relied on.

steps.label: Making diversity
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the formula predicts 99.99% while the actual vote gets only 87.7% because the errors are shared. This page asks how to make members differ. Diversity is how different the members' decisions are, and one measure is V: the fraction of members whose decision differs from the majority. The three routes are the source's: the same feature space but different data points, which is bootstrap resampling with replacement and works best for unstable trees; different classifier types; different feature subspaces. The experiment was designed for this lecture and generated by code: 10-dimensional data with a random class, coordinates 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 shifted by 0.9 times the class and the other 5 pure noise; 150 training points, seeds 200 to 214, 15 times; 2000 fixed new points. A single depth-3 tree gets 71.2%; 11 bootstrap trees get 77.9 plus or minus 2.1% with V equal to 0.197; 11 trees each with 4 random coordinates get 75.9 plus or minus 2.3% with V equal to 0.241; 5 classifier types get 82.1 plus or minus 1.2% with V equal to 0.114. The largest V is not the most accurate; the 5 types include a logistic fit that happens to suit this data, so this does not show that different types are always better. The next page asks which combination rule to use.

steps.label: The Bayesian view
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page looked at three routes to diversity, and the largest V is not the most accurate. This page asks which combination rule to use. The Bayesian view: assume the x j seen by the classifiers are independent; the Bayes rule gives P of omega k to the power 1 minus L times the product of the classifiers' posteriors, maximised over k, which is again a product rule but very sensitive to errors in the posterior estimates; the sum tolerates errors better and often beats the product in practice, as the source reports from Kittler and colleagues. The conclusions of the source's handwritten-digit experiment: no rule is always best; in some cases the combination is worse than the best single classifier; combining the same classifier on different feature sets works best. This lecture saw the same: on the first page the vote of three at 86.2% is below 3-NN at 87.8%, and on the seventh page the random-feature-subset vote was the worst. To remember: the sum and the majority vote are the most used; there is no panacea theorem. This is the last page of the main line. The next page is an extension: what the sum and the product do when outliers appear.

steps.label: Extension: the median
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said no rule is always best. This extension page asks what the sum and the product do when outlying outputs appear. The median rule takes the median of the classifiers' probabilities and then picks the largest class. The example was designed for this lecture: five classifiers give omega 1 the values 0.80, 0.85, 0.75, 0.01 and 0.01, the rest going to omega 2. Sum: omega 1 is 0.484 and omega 2 is 0.516, so omega 2 is chosen, wrong. Product: omega 1 is 5.1 times 10 to the minus 5 and omega 2 is 7.4 times 10 to the minus 3, so omega 2 is chosen, wrong. Median: omega 1 is 0.75 and omega 2 is 0.25, so omega 1 is chosen, right. With outliers the sum is pulled away by the extreme values and the median stays steady. The source also mentions max, min and median with the chain of inequalities: product at most min at most mean at most max. The next page has two exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the median is steadier with outlying outputs. This page is the exercises. Exercise 1: every classifier is right with probability p equal to 0.7 and the decisions are independent; what is the majority-vote accuracy for L equal to 3? The hint is that l c is 2, so add up at least 2 right. Exercise 2: with the same p equal to 0.7, what is the accuracy for L equal to 5, and how much more than L equal to 3? The hint is that l c is 3, so add three terms. Work them out first; the next page is the worked solution.

steps.label: Extension: worked solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page set two exercises on majority voting. Exercise 1: L equal to 3 and l c equal to 2: 3 times 0.7 squared times 0.3 is 0.441, plus 0.7 cubed, 0.343, gives 0.784. Exercise 2: L equal to 5 and l c equal to 3: 10 times 0.7 cubed times 0.3 squared is 0.3087; plus 5 times 0.7 to the fourth times 0.3, which is 0.36015; plus 0.7 to the fifth, which is 0.16807; the total is 0.837, which is 0.053 more than L equal to 3. Check: 0.7 to 0.784 to 0.837 rises monotonically, but only under independence; real dependent classifiers do not rise this much. This is the last page of KP24; the next KP is the following unit of chapter 4.
